newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta counts vote on Europe after record turnout.
newsitem.headline: Malta counts vote on Europe after record turnout.

text.p: Election officials surrounded by tight security worked through Sunday to count votes after a record turnout in Malta's general election which will decide whether the Mediterranean island joins the European Union.
Early on Sunday chief electoral commissioner Carmell Portelli told a news conference that 97 percent of the nearly 275,000 electorate voted in Saturday's poll.
At stake is the future of Malta's application to join the EU, to be pursued if the former ruling Nationalist Party wins, and scrapped if the opposition Labour Party achieves victory.
Malta has no independent opinion polls and both main parties say their own polls show they will win.
Around the counting centre, near the old Arab walled city of Mdina, heavily armed troops manned checkpoints up to one km (half a mile) away, checking passes and scrutinising cars.
Results were not expected to be known until late on Sunday or early on Monday, despite repeated complaints about the slowness of counting after polling stations closed at 10 p.m.
The Sunday Times said both the turnout and incident-free vote "shows that voters could make their all-important choice responsibly, without fear or favour".
Elections in the 1970s and 1980s were marked by violent clashes which both parties pledged to avoid, the Labour Party banning its supporters from putting up banners to avoid strife.
Reflecting the intimate nature of the island, election manifestos ranged from international to very local issues.
But, in a country where normally only about 5,000 votes separate the parties and turnout has traditionally topped 90 percent, the focus was Europe and its impact on the economy.
Prime Minister Edward Fenech Adami, 62, who had a three-seat majority in the 65-member parliament, is pledged to pursue the EU membership application he made in 1990.
He told Reuters on the eve of voting: "I already have a mandate...(but) it will be a sort of another referendum on Malta's membership of the EU."
Labour leader Alfred Sant, 48, opposes membership.

He says it does not suit the small island and Value Added Tax (VAT) at 15 percent standard pushed up living costs, brought hardship to ordinary people, and was imposed purely to please Europe. "No other country imposed VAT even before serious negotiations on entry," he said.
For Fenech Adami, Europe "is the only way Malta can go, in our own best interests". He sees EU talks completed and Malta ready for membership by mid-1998.
Labour seeks instead a "special relationship" and what it terms "positive neutrality" being best suited to the island where sovereignty is a sensitive issue.
The Nationalists believe membership will bring reassurance to Malta, sited in an area Fenech Adami terms as "turbulent".

Labour, already alarmed at increased visits by Western naval vessels, fears Malta -- awarded the British George Cross in 1942 for its bravery withstanding Italian and German wartime attacks -- being turned back to a fortress island.
Sant told Reuters that pulling out of NATO's Partnership for Peace Programme, which Malta joined in 1995, "will be my first priority".
It would be followed by legislation to abolish VAT and replace it with customs tariffs, undercutting a basis of EU membership and signalling Malta's withdrawal of its bid.
One possibility suggested by political correspondent Anthony Manduca, of the Malta Independent, was neither main party getting an absolute majority.
An unknown element is the Democratic Alternative, which won no seats in 1992. It favours EU membership in principle but says a referendum should decide after all conditions are known.
It complained early on Sunday that it had been refused permission to have delegates in the hall to scrutinise voting.
Portelli said that under the law only parties represented in parliament had this right: "We have to abide by the law."
